text.en: Asha's teacher held up a thin book. "This guides the whole country," she said.

The Constitution of India is the supreme law. It was drafted by the Constituent Assembly, with Dr B. R. Ambedkar as chairman of the Drafting Committee, adopted on 26 November 1949 and brought into force in most respects on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.
The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic and promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. The Fundamental Rights are guaranteed by the Constitution, and Directive Principles guide the government.
Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their responsibilities. The Constitution can be amended, but the Supreme Court’s basic structure doctrine limits that power. Parliament cannot destroy or damage the Constitution’s basic structure. India has a federal structure with a strong centre.
The Constitution of India is the supreme law.

board.text: Constitution

text.en: The Constituent Assembly debated and adopted the Constitution. Its Drafting Committee prepared a draft for the Assembly to consider.

board.text: Constituent Assembly

text.en: Doctor B R Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

board.text: Preamble

text.en: The Assembly adopted the Constitution on twenty-six November nineteen forty-nine. Most of it came into force on twenty-six January nineteen fifty, the date remembered as Republic Day.

board.text: Fundamental Rights

text.en: The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic and promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

board.text: Directive Principles

text.en: The Fundamental Rights are guaranteed by the Constitution, and Directive Principles guide the government.

board.text: Fundamental Duties

text.en: Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their responsibilities.

board.text: Constitution

text.en: Parliament can amend the Constitution. The Supreme Court’s basic structure doctrine limits that power: an amendment cannot destroy or damage the Constitution’s basic structure.

board.text: Constituent Assembly

text.en: A constitution says how public institutions are formed, what powers they have and what limits apply. It provides a framework for ordinary laws.

board.text: A constitution sets up public institutions

text.en: Members discussed proposals and changed the wording before adopting the document. A committee prepares a draft, while the Assembly makes the decision.

board.text: The Constituent Assembly debated the draft

text.en: On twenty-six November nineteen forty-nine, the Assembly adopted the Constitution. Most of it began to operate on twenty-six January nineteen fifty.

board.text: Adoption and commencement are different

text.en: The Preamble opens with We, the People of India. It sets out the kind of republic the Constitution establishes and the goals it seeks.

board.text: The Preamble expresses constitutional ideals

text.en: Sovereignty concerns India’s authority to govern itself. Democratic government draws its authority from the people.

board.text: Sovereign and democratic describe political authority

text.en: India’s President holds an elected constitutional office. The position does not pass from one person to another by inheritance.

board.text: A republic has a constitutional head of state

text.en: People may hold different beliefs. The Constitution protects freedom of conscience and religious practice within its stated limits.

board.text: Secularism and freedom of conscience

text.en: Justice concerns fair treatment. Liberty protects freedoms, equality concerns equal standing, and fraternity calls for a shared sense of belonging.

board.text: Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity are distinct

text.en: They protect people and, in some cases, citizens specifically. The scope and conditions depend on the article.

board.text: Fundamental Rights are in Part Three

text.en: Equality before the law is protected by Article Fourteen. Article Nineteen protects several freedoms for citizens subject to constitutionally permitted restrictions.

board.text: Equality and freedoms have practical meanings

text.en: Article Twenty-One protects life and personal liberty. Article Twenty-One A provides for free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen.

board.text: Life and liberty, and education

text.en: The Constitution protects against exploitation, protects religious freedom, and protects cultural and educational interests.

board.text: Rights cover other kinds of protection too

text.en: Article Thirty-Two provides a remedy through the Supreme Court for enforcing Fundamental Rights. High Courts can also issue writs under Article Two Hundred and Twenty-Six.

board.text: Courts can enforce Fundamental Rights

text.en: Part Four gives public authorities goals such as promoting welfare. Courts do not directly enforce the principles as rights.

board.text: Directive Principles guide policy and laws

text.en: Part Four A lists duties for citizens. Examples include respecting the Constitution and protecting the natural environment.

board.text: Fundamental Duties describe civic responsibilities

text.en: A right protects a person’s freedom or interest. A Directive Principle guides the State. A duty describes a responsibility of a citizen.

board.text: Compare the three by their functions

text.en: Part Two addresses citizenship at the start of the Constitution. It also gives Parliament power to make laws on citizenship.

board.text: The Constitution provides for citizenship at its commencement

text.en: The Seventh Schedule lists subjects for the Union, states and both. Defence is a Union List example. Public health is generally a State List subject.

board.text: The Union and states share lawmaking powers

text.en: Education is on the Concurrent List. Both levels can legislate on listed topics, subject to the Constitution’s rules about overlaps and conflicts.

board.text: A Concurrent List subject can involve both levels

text.en: The Constitution distinguishes a national emergency, provisions for failure of constitutional machinery in a state, and a financial emergency. Each has its own conditions and safeguards.

board.text: Emergency provisions have different purposes

text.en: Article Three Hundred and Sixty-Eight provides a process for constitutional amendments. Some amendments also need ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.

board.text: Amendment and basic structure go together

text.en: Find the relevant article or part, and ask how it works. A short slogan can miss a right’s limits, a duty’s audience or a policy principle’s role.

board.text: Read a constitutional claim with its source

text.en: India is sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic and a republic.
It promises justice, liberty, equality, fraternity.
It gives the aims of the Constitution.

problem.en: A student says the Constitution was adopted on Republic Day. How can you correct the timeline?

text.en: Place adoption on 26 November 1949.

why.en: The Constituent Assembly adopted the final text on that date.

text.en: Place general commencement on 26 January 1950.

why.en: Most provisions took effect then, which Republic Day commemorates.

problem.en: How do equality before the law and a goal to promote public welfare differ?

text.en: Equality before the law is a Fundamental Right.

why.en: A court can enforce constitutional rights in an appropriate case.

text.en: Promoting public welfare is a goal of the Directive Principles.

why.en: Directive Principles guide law and policy but are not directly enforceable as rights.

problem.en: Why can both Parliament and a state legislature deal with education?

text.en: Education appears on the Concurrent List.

why.en: The Constitution assigns some lawmaking subject areas to both levels.

text.en: Read the constitutional rules if their laws conflict.

why.en: The shared lawmaking field has rules for resolving inconsistency.

prompt.en: A friend says The Constitution came into force on 15 August 1947. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: It came into force on 26 January 1950.

points.en: Adopted 26 November 1949. Most provisions came into force on 26 January 1950.
